tier_reason: Benchmark code is public in benchmark/ (benchmark_micro.hpp, benchmark_selective.hpp, CMakeLists.txt, build.sh), and the README states clang 20.1.8, -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto, and an AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U. It compares directly against std::vector with std::allocator and against std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource. Flags are stated, so the >50x cap does not apply.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline: up to 1300x faster construction and reserve() than std::vector and up to 3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector. Results image: reserve microbenchmark 939.81x-1380.19x faster than std::vector (one outlier of 4762.93x at large2) and 2.65x-3.63x faster than pmr::vector; emplace 1.20x-1.61x faster than std; selective construct path 1.21x-15.40x faster than std; churn simulation ranges from 1.58x slower to 1.66x faster than std; raw alloc 1.81x-287.40x faster than malloc.
corrections.caveats: The ~1000x+ figures come only from the reserve microbenchmark, where each frame creates one std::vector, calls reserve(count), and frees it. glibc malloc/free of large blocks likely dominates that path, so it is not general alloc/free churn. In the more realistic tables the gains shrink to 1.2x-1.6x (emplace), and churn simulation is 1.06x-1.58x slower than std for 4096B and 16384B elements. Results are published only as a PNG image. New project (created Aug 2025, 37 stars) with no independent verification found.

notes: Headline numbers match the README text and the results image. baseline_stdlib = libstdc++ is inferred: build.sh adds -stdlib=libc++ only on macOS, and the test system is Arch Linux clang, which defaults to libstdc++. Per-case numbers were read from the results PNG (https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c7692e54-...).

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper compares Hoard against the Solaris 7 default allocator and Ptmalloc (glibc) on a 14-way Sun Enterprise 5000 with GNU C++ -O6. The compiler version is unstated and the benchmark code is not tied to the paper, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator on 14 processors, and up to 18x over the next best allocator tested. At 14 processors: Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc, threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc, shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc. Uniprocessor: BEMengine 10.3% faster than the Solaris allocator, but the average over the uniprocessor benchmarks is 6.2% slower than Solaris.
corrections.caveats: Primary evidence is the ASPLOS 2000 paper, run on 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC with Solaris 7 against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era; the GNU C++ version is unstated. Uniprocessor, Hoard averaged 6.2% slower than the Solaris allocator (shbench +49.2%, espresso +15.9%, Ghostscript +10.6% runtime). The current README adds first-party modern results (code in benchmarks/, 192-core 2-node AMD EPYC, exact CPU model, compiler, and flags unstated, charts only). Those results claim 1.3-1.5x higher Larson throughput than glibc, mimalloc, and jemalloc, and 1.6x faster than glibc at 128 threads on NUMA. The README concedes that jemalloc wins linux-scalability. Hoard is also in daanx/mimalloc-bench as 'hd', but those results are chart images only.

notes: The old record had '10.6% faster (BEMengine)'. The paper's BEMengine figure is 10.3% faster; 10.6% is Ghostscript, where Hoard is slower. The earlier caveat said no modern reproduction exists, but the README now has modern first-party benchmarks against glibc. Those are tier C material, so the paper keeps this entry at B.

tier_reason: First-party QuickBench numbers compare against std::vector with the default allocator (glibc malloc). The code is public (arena-benchmark.cpp and the QuickBench links), and the QuickBench options show clang 17.0 -O3 with libstdc++. The CPU model is unknown (shared AWS pool), so it cannot be A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 17.0, -O3, -std=c++20, libstdc++ ('gnu' lib), per the QuickBench options of the linked benchmarks (not stated in the README)
corrections.hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool: the QuickBench result context shows 1 CPU at 2300 MHz, 32KB L1d, 256KB L2, 45MB L3; CPU model unstated. The README includes QuickBench's disclaimer that absolute timings are unreliable.
corrections.caveats: The README does not state compiler or flags, but the QuickBench runs used clang 17.0 -O3 with libstdc++. The CPU model is unknown and QuickBench's shared AWS pool makes absolute durations unreliable, so it stays at Tier C. The 93x-230x ratios for 1KB-8KB objects coincide with crossing glibc's mmap threshold (as the README explains), so they are not a general allocator speed claim. The arena cannot free non-top allocations. There is no LICENSE file, so usability is 'reference' only.

notes: All README table numbers match (2.2x-4.4x up to 512B; 93x, 150x, 190x, 230x for 1K-8K). Compiler and flags were retrieved from the QuickBench API (quick-bench.com/quick/<id>). The Show HN post exists (2025-03-13, 2 points).

tier_reason: The smmalloc README table compares ltalloc against crt (the default runtime malloc) on i7-2600/Windows 10 and PS4, but compiler, flags, and units are unstated. The smmalloc repo's current perf code no longer includes ltalloc. ltalloc's own README table is first-party with partial methodology. Both are C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On Windows 10/i7-2600: ~2.6x faster than crt single-threaded (62,525,965 vs 23,853,865) and ~1.9x at 5 threads (27,333,887 vs 14,636,381) (derived from page data). On PS4: ~6.4x faster than crt single-threaded (28,571,429 vs 4,444,444) and ~44x at 4 threads (14,683,637 vs 332,095) (derived from page data). Units are not stated on the page (higher is better).
corrections.caveats: The main numbers come from the third-party smmalloc README table: compiler, flags, and units are unstated, the workload is not described on the page, and the current smmalloc perf code no longer benchmarks ltalloc. On the i7-2600 table, ltalloc trails rpmalloc, hoard, and smmalloc. The earlier caveat was wrong: ltalloc's own README FAQ does have a first-party results table, published as an image. That table covers 128-byte alloc/free from concurrent threads on several Windows/Linux machines, with the default allocator 6.21x-218.75x slower than ltalloc (i7 2600/Win7 single-thread: 16.0 vs 165.0 M ops/s per thread). The linked Xeon/Debian chart (googlecode) is dead. The repo has commits in 2026 and is not GitHub-archived or a fork.

notes: Numbers match the smmalloc table, but the record's ratios were not marked as derived, so they are now tagged. benchmark_url is left as smmalloc (text table). The ltalloc README table (https://i.imgur.com/fiR9C9M.png) is an alternative first-party source with larger ratios, but its flags are unstated and some ratios are >50x.

tier_reason: The project's own rpmalloc-benchmark suite (code public, benchmark/ with crt, jemalloc, and others) plots rpmalloc against crt (glibc malloc) on Ubuntu 16.10. CPU model, compiler, and flags are not stated, and results are chart images only, so it is C.

corrections.baseline: crt (system glibc malloc on Ubuntu 16.10, backing operator new/delete); charts also include tcmalloc, ptmalloc3, jemalloc, lockfree-malloc, scalloc, lockless
corrections.claimed_speedup: Page text: rpmalloc is faster than all tested allocators except lockfree-malloc in a few cases when threads exceed cores; tcmalloc and jemalloc trail behind ~15%. Versus crt (glibc malloc), charts show about 2.3x at 1 thread and 3.4x at 4 threads in random [16,1000]B, and about 2.4x at 1 thread in [512,160000]B (derived from page data, read approximately from chart images).
corrections.hardware: Ubuntu 16.10 machine with 8 logical cores (4 physical + HT) and 12GiB RAM; CPU model not stated. Windows 10 and macOS results are listed as 'coming soon' and are not published.
corrections.caveats: Results come from the project's own suite. CPU model, compiler, and flags are not stated, and only Ubuntu 16.10 chart images are published, so ratios are approximate readings. Hoard is in the suite's code but not in the published charts. The page's 'faster than all except lockfree-malloc' text is contradicted in the [512,160000]B chart: 'lockless' beats rpmalloc at 1 thread (~14.5 vs ~8.9 M ops/CPU-s) and roughly ties it at higher thread counts. rpmalloc also appears in daanx/mimalloc-bench as 'rp', but only as chart images whose allocator legend is not in the image.

notes: The claim text matches BENCHMARKS.md, but no numbers vs crt appear in text. The crt ratios come from 2 of the chart images and are marked approximate. Hoard was removed from the baseline list because it does not appear in the published charts. Repo metadata checks out (MIT, 2,508 stars, last commit 2026-07-15).
